work_order.understanding: Issue #97 carries three non-blocking review findings on PR #94 (for #88), all confined to ReportTableList.test.tsx. ReportTableList.tsx:84 (`key={category.uncategorizedId ?? category.id}`) is correct and stays byte-for-byte unchanged — the ticket asks whether the tests can detect a wrong key expression, not whether the expression is wrong. I reproduced all three findings on current main: baseline is 4/4 green; `key={category.uncategorizedId}` (the `?? category.id` fallback deleted) leaves all 4 green; `key={category.id}` (pre-fix) fails only tests 1 and 2; and `/Encountered two children with the same key/i` is strictly subsumed by `/same key/i`. The v2 plan was rejected for one reason: its test accounting was self-contradictory. files[] said test 2 was renamed and stripped down to the same assertions as test 1, out_of_scope said it was deleted, and test 1 was never mentioned at all — so following files[] literally produced 4 tests, while every acceptance number assumed 3. That objection is correct and I have resolved it the way it prescribed: test 2 is DELETED outright in files[] and removed from tests[], test 1 survives unchanged as the synthetic-rows collision guard, test 4 is renamed and repaired, and test 3 moves to the new file. That is 2 tests in ReportTableList.test.tsx + 1 in ReportTableList.missingKey.test.tsx = 3, and I built the whole thing and ran it: 3 passed across 2 files, with the mutant matrix landing on exactly the counts every criterion already states.
work_order.root_cause: Two independent defects, and fixing the filter alone fixes neither. (1) The console.error filter is pinned to React's duplicate-key phrasing, so a MISSING key — what a deleted `?? category.id` fallback produces for real categories, which have no uncategorizedId — is a different sentence the filter never matches. (2) The missing-key assertion is inherently order-dependent within a file, because React emits that sentence at most once per TEST FILE; I measured this directly (one keyless fixture rendered by three tests in a single file gave missing=1, missing=0, missing=0). Whichever test renders first consumes the file's warning budget, so a second test asserting on it passes vacuously no matter what the key expression does. (3) A fixture whose sibling keys cannot collide under any expression constrains nothing. The fix therefore separates the two warning classes into two files rather than widening one filter.
work_order.approach: Split the file by warning class rather than widening a single filter, because the two React sentences behave differently: the duplicate-key warning repeats freely, the missing-key warning fires once per test file. (1) Narrow DUPLICATE_KEY_WARNINGS to a single `DUPLICATE_KEY_WARNING = /same key/i` — the second entry was strictly subsumed — and rewrite the comment to record why loose tail-matching exists and that the exact-sentence pattern was removed precisely because it added nothing. (2) Move the missing-key guard into a NEW file, ReportTableList.missingKey.test.tsx, matching `/unique .?key.? prop/i`, whose comment records the measured once-per-file behaviour so the deleted-fallback mutant fails reliably rather than only when that test happens to run first. (3) DELETE test 2 outright rather than renaming it. It read the fixture through a renderRowSpy, returning ['other','transfer','off_budget'] for any implementation whatsoever, and once its spy and its two uncategorizedId assertions are stripped its remaining body is byte-for-byte identical to test 1 — keeping a renamed copy would leave two identical tests and break the 3-test accounting every acceptance criterion states. (4) Rename test 4 to 'logs no duplicate-key error when real categories and synthetic rows are siblings' and repair its fixture by adding transferRow as a second synthetic sibling plus a matching getByText('Transfers') assertion; I verified that under `key={category.id}` the repaired fixture reports dup=1 where the one-synthetic-row original reports dup=0, so it finally has discriminating power. Add a comment above each surviving test naming which half of the expression it guards and which mutant kills it. (5) Fix a latent type bug the edits expose: the fixture helpers spell `totalDebits`/`netDebits` but GroupedEntity/DataEntity declare `totalDebts`/`netDebts`; I confirmed that restoring the misspelling produces 2 TS2561 errors, invisible on main only because tsc-strict checks changed files.

risks: The change is test-only and touches no production code, so the risk to the app is nil. The risk is in the tests themselves: patterns written too loosely could match an unrelated console.error and fail the suite spuriously, and patterns written too tightly would fail open again — the exact defect this ticket exists to fix. Both patterns are anchored on React's distinctive wording.

Because the filters are now split by file, a missing key elsewhere inside ReportTableList's subtree is caught only by ReportTableList.missingKey.test.tsx, and only the FIRST such key in that file. A second independent keyless list added later would not be caught by adding a second test to that file — it needs the existing test's fixture widened, or a new file. The comment above the filter records this.

The once-per-file suppression is React-internal and could change across React versions. If a future React emits the missing-key warning per-render again, the split-file design remains correct and merely becomes more conservative than necessary. The reverse (React dropping the warning entirely) would silently void the guard, which is true of any console.error-based approach.

work_order.confidence_rationale: Every number in this order is a measurement I took by building the proposed design and running it, not an inference carried over from the rejected v2 plan. Baseline 4/4 green on main, all three review findings reproduced, the once-per-file missing-key warning measured (missing=1, missing=0, missing=0 for three renders of one keyless fixture in one file), the repaired mixed-sibling fixture confirmed to report dup=1 under `key={category.id}` where the shipped one-synthetic-row fixture reports dup=0, and the full six-mutant matrix landing exactly on the counts AC-1/AC-2/AC-3 state: baseline 3 passed; `key={category.id}` 2 of 3; `key={category.uncategorizedId}` 1 of 3; `key={category.id ?? category.uncategorizedId}` 2 of 3; `key={category.name}` and `key={category.uncategorizedId || category.id}` green as behaviourally equivalent. Order-independence was verified by actually swapping the two tests and re-running. typecheck, lint, and the wider reports suite (30 files, 499 tests) are all clean. The 7 points held back are for what no local run settles: whether a future React could reword these sentences or change the dedup behaviour, and whether a browser QA pass would surface anything this test-file change does not already cover.
evidence: Baseline on main: `yarn workspace @actual-app/web vitest --run ReportTableList` → Tests 4 passed (4), 1 file.
Finding A reproduced: with ReportTableList.tsx:84 mutated to `key={category.uncategorizedId}`, the same probe measured missing=1, dup=0 — a real sentence the shipped filter never matches.

Missing-key warning fires ONCE PER TEST FILE, not per render pass. Three separate tests in one file rendering the identical keyless fixture gave missing=1, missing=0, missing=0. So whichever test renders first consumes the file's budget and every later one asserting on it passes vacuously. This is why the guard needs its own file.

Finding C reproduced and the repair verified: with `key={category.id}`, the shipped one-synthetic-row mixed fixture reports dup=0 (no discriminating power), while the repaired fixture carrying uncategorizedRow AND transferRow reports dup=1. The second synthetic sibling is what makes it fail.
Finding B reproduced: `/Encountered two children with the same key/i` is strictly subsumed by `/same key/i` — every string it matches contains 'same key' — so it is deleted.

Order-independence measured: with the two tests in ReportTableList.test.tsx physically swapped, `key={category.uncategorizedId}` still yields 'Tests 1 failed | 2 passed (3)', the failure being 'keys real category rows that have no uncategorizedId'.

Final mutant matrix for this design, each run end to end: baseline 3 passed; `key={category.id}` fails 2 of 3 (both collision tests, named individually); `key={category.uncategorizedId}` fails 1 of 3 ('keys real category rows that have no uncategorizedId'); `key={category.id ?? category.uncategorizedId}` fails 2 of 3; `key={category.name}` and `key={category.uncategorizedId || category.id}` stay green as behaviourally equivalent.

Latent type bug confirmed: restoring `totalDebits`/`netDebits` in the fixture helpers produces 'error TS2561: Object literal may only specify known properties, but totalDebits does not exist in type GroupedEntity' at line 30 and the DataEntity equivalent at line 44. GroupedEntity/DataEntity declare `totalDebts`/`netDebts`.
Gates green after the change: `yarn typecheck` clean (10/10 tasks, 39s), `yarn lint` clean (2547 files), wider reports suite 30 files / 499 tests passed.
`git status --porcelain` shows only ReportTableList.test.tsx (modified) and ReportTableList.missingKey.test.tsx (new) — ReportTableList.tsx is byte-for-byte unchanged from main.

alternatives_considered.approach: Keep one file, widen the filter to [/same key/i, /unique .?key.? prop/i], and let the uuid test guard the deleted fallback — the remedy the v2 rejection prescribed.
alternatives_considered.rejected_because: It is correct only by accident of ordering. React emits the missing-key warning at most once per test file, which I measured: one keyless fixture rendered from three tests in a single file gave exactly one warning. Whichever test renders first consumes it, so the guard dies silently if anyone adds a render above it or reorders the file. Splitting the assertion into its own file fixes the mechanism rather than accommodating it, and it also removes the temptation to assert the missing-key sentence from two tests in one file, which can never work.

alternatives_considered.approach: Keep the fixture-reading test as a renamed second copy of the collision guard, as files[] in v2 instructed, making the suite 4 tests.
alternatives_considered.rejected_because: Rejected twice over. Once its renderRowSpy and its two uncategorizedId assertions are stripped — which is what made it assert nothing about keys — its remaining body is byte-for-byte the first test, so the file would hold the same test twice. And it would force AC-1, AC-2, AC-3 and the whole mutant matrix to be restated at 4 tests when the criterion set already describes 3 and every other number in it is verified. Deleting it outright is the resolution the v2 rejection named as cheapest, and it is now stated in files[] as well as out_of_scope so the three parts of the document agree.

alternatives_considered.approach: Reset React's module-level warning suppression between tests so one file could hold both guards, instead of splitting into two files.
alternatives_considered.rejected_because: React exposes no supported way to reset the warning dedup; it would mean reaching into React internals or resetting modules between tests, coupling the suite to an implementation detail of a specific React version that would break the moment that detail changes. A second file costs one duplicated fixture helper pair and depends on nothing but Vitest's default per-file module isolation.

alternatives_considered.approach: Assert on the key expression directly, by capturing the keys React receives instead of watching console.error.
alternatives_considered.rejected_because: React keeps keys internal to its reconciler and does not expose them to renderRow, which is exactly why the file reads console.error in the first place. A DevTools fiber walk or a jsx-runtime mock would couple the test to React internals and to the react-compiler transform, both of which change under this repo's setup; a broken transform would then break the guard rather than the code.

alternatives_considered.approach: Delete the mixed-sibling test outright, as the reviewer's first option permits, rather than repairing it.
alternatives_considered.rejected_because: A repaired fixture is strictly better and I verified it kills `key={category.id}` (dup=1, versus dup=0 for the shipped one-synthetic-row version). Deleting would leave no coverage of a real category sharing one parent with synthetic rows — a list shape the production query layer does produce. The repair costs one added fixture row and one added assertion.

work_order.debate_summary: The brief carried one binding objection against v2, and it was a bookkeeping one, not a design one: files[] said the fixture-reading test was renamed and stripped to test 1's assertions, out_of_scope said it was deleted, and test 1 was never mentioned at all — so an implementer following files[] literally would ship 4 tests while every acceptance number said 3. I took the objection's own cheapest resolution and applied it everywhere at once: test 2 is deleted outright (stated in files[], removed from tests[], and its rationale kept in out_of_scope), test 1 survives unchanged as the synthetic-rows collision guard, test 4 is renamed and repaired with a second synthetic sibling, and test 3 moves to the new missing-key file. That is 2 + 1 = 3, so AC-1, AC-2, AC-3 and qa_script step 1 stand unedited. I then rebuilt the whole design and re-measured everything rather than trusting v2's numbers: baseline 3 passed across 2 files, `key={category.id}` fails 2 of 3, `key={category.uncategorizedId}` fails 1 of 3, the two equivalent mutants stay green, and swapping the two tests leaves the missing-key guard still failing exactly one test. The one design question v2 raised — that React emits the missing-key warning once per test FILE, making any single-file guard order-dependent — I re-verified from scratch (missing=1, missing=0, missing=0 across three renders in one file) and it held.
